utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, you were to the left part -- you were to the left of this shop window, in front of its left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I was standing in front of the shop window. Now exactly, I wouldn't know the exact spot. Well, where it is marked number 1. That is where I stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the left part of the shop window. More precisely, slightly to the right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look at this shop window closely. You have the photograph on the screen as well, I think. Could you tell us, in what part of the window did the bullet hit it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I'm not sure. This happened in a very short period of time. I went into shock, so I don't know exactly where it hit. Logically, it hit the window because I was standing next to the shop window and the bullet went through my stomach. It didn't stick there. And I didn't go back to this location, so I'm unable to say where exactly it hit the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, Witness, you have just said, and this is on page 46, that the bullet hit the window. Are you confirming that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: One could hear the glass breaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you closely examine the photograph, please. And after examining it, will you tell me that the glass behind the grid, is the glass in any way broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No, I can't see that it is broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the ground just in front... The part of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you identify here pieces of glass, broken glass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't see any. And it's not a clear photograph anyway, so you can't see very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, could you please remove from the ELMO the photograph and show it to the witness in the original, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No, I don't see any pieces of glass here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the photo was shown to the witness close up and that -- the left part of the shop window was zoomed in on, and no bullet impact could be seen on the glass of the shop window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it possible that when you heard glass breaking, that this breaking of glass was not the glass of the shop window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I'm telling you this happened in a second, in a very short span of time. And we took shelter in the passageway. There was a big hullabaloo around us, so I can't tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you affirm that you were shot at. Is this something that you stand by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't shoot at myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you were shot at and if the bullet, after passing through your body, ended up in the window, how can you explain that the glass is not broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Maybe a hole was left in the glass. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see this hole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No. I'm saying this happened in a matter of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you see a hole on the photograph that was shown to you a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, I should like to go back to the street and what happened during this incident. We know that, next to this shop, there was a restaurant. Could you tell us the name of that restaurant? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If I mentioned the word "Arijana," does that remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Today it is called Arijana. I don't know whether that was what it was then. I just didn't pay any attention at the time. I just looked at the shop window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. So the name of the restaurant was Arijana. I think we can consider that to have been established. When you arrived in front of this shop window, did you pass by the Arijana restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, because we were moving from that direction. My mother and sister stopped in front of the shop window, and for a while I continued riding my bicycle on the platform in front, and then I too stopped in front of the window when the wounding occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, opposite the restaurant, there's a parking place. We saw that a moment ago on the photograph. In relation to that parking, were there any military vehicles at the time parked in that parking lot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, but I'm saying again I just didn't pay any attention. We were walking by. We were going to see a relative. I didn't look to see whether there were any military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen civilian vehicles used by the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, because that was normal. There was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, were there civilian vehicles on this parking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were immediately taken by somebody to a civilian vehicle after being wounded. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes. This man came from the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. How, Witness, did you know that that vehicle was not a vehicle used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So when you say that it was a civilian vehicle, in fact you can't know whether it was used for civilian or for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I saw that man for the first time in my life, so I don't know whether he was a military man or a civilian, whether his car was a military vehicle or not. I saw him for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're creating confusion to the witness at this very moment. One of your questions was: "Have you ever seen civilian vehicles used by the military?" That clearly indicates that the use of a vehicle by the military does not change it to be a civilian vehicle. Otherwise, your question is without any sense. It is unfair later to put to the witness that when he talks about civilian vehicles, to give the words "civilian vehicle" a different meaning from the meaning you used yourself. If you're aiming at establishing that during this period of time, in that situation, vehicles that looked -- were not -- could not be distinguished from other civilian vehicles would be used by military, then the question is whether this would be the most suitable witness to put that to, apart from whether there has not already been evidence in this court that -- at least some testimony whether that was done. And I do not know whether this is in dispute. I do not know whether it is in dispute that in this situation civilian vehicles would be used sometimes for -- by the military and perhaps for military purposes. I do not know. I'm just looking to Mr. Ierace. But if this is in dispute, of course you could continue your line of questioning, but it should be fair to the witness. You cannot use words, when you speak to him yourself, in a different meaning and then confront the witness with the problem that they might have another meaning as well. He used his words in exactly the same way you did it yourself. I see no response from Mr. Ierace. That means that it is in dispute that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm trying to recall whether we've had any evidence to that effect. I don't recollect any to the effect that civilian vehicles were used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, military -- I didn't say "military purposes," I think. I think I said that were used by military men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't recall any evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But stay away from that. Please then proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I apologise, Mr. President. It is true that sometimes that the polemics is semantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To make myself quite clear, this vehicle that you took, in a sense, to go to the hospital, were there any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: You must understand, I was wounded. I was in a state of shock. I wasn't up to looking around whether there were any weapons. All I cared about was saving my life. I didn't care whether there were any weapons there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm fully aware of what this must have meant for you, but it is up to all of us to try and understand the totality of all these problems. So if you saw any weapons in that vehicle, small or big ones, you should say so. So did you see any weapons in that vehicle? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have nothing to fear from your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you didn't see any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I come back to the question of the restaurant now. When you passed in front of the Arijana, the restaurant in question, were you able to see whether there were several people inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you were wounded, immediately after that, did many people come out of that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I know that while I was standing next to the shop window, that there were children there. I don't know exactly how many. And immediately after I was wounded, with my mother and sister, entered the passageway and that is when that man came up. That's all I'm able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You didn't see any other people coming out of the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there any police in the street at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, but I must say again, I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether, as you went along, you came across a police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember. This was eight years ago, so I can't tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. A question was put to you by the Prosecution regarding the presence of any military objects, and you said that you were not certain and that you didn't pay any attention to that. You told us that several times. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is it possible then to deduce from your answer that there may have been a military presence but that you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I didn't notice. But a war was on, so it would be quite normal, though I didn't pay any attention, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that that would have been quite normal, are you telling us that it was often that you would see soldiers in the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I can't tell you with certainty. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did you say that this would be normal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't mean -- but there was a war. There was civilians, of course, and there were people who were protecting their entrances and so on. So in a sense, it was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You said a moment ago that at the beginning of these events, people organised themselves as defence squads for their buildings, to guard them, and you told us that these persons owned and even manufactured their weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I didn't see that with my own eyes because I was mostly in the cellar, inside. I didn't go out. So that is what people were saying after the war, that they made their own weapons and so on. But this is not something that I saw, and I can't tell you with certainty. I was mostly in the basement because I was still a child. I didn't dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, why did you spend your days in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Because it wasn't safe to walk around. They were shelling. They were shooting. That is why we were in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, Witness, you didn't go to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Until April 1992, while I was in Sarajevo, I didn't. But after 1994, I did because the school was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Because there was shooting. It wasn't safe to leave the house at all. This was the beginning of the war. At the beginning of the war, all schools stopped working. And later on, they resumed working at some locations and in some houses. But at the beginning of the war, the schools stopped working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Again, there has been evidence called on this issue by the Prosecution which has not been the subject of any challenge by the Defence. I take it it's not in dispute from -- I take that from the behaviour of the Defence in the past. Therefore, this line of questioning would appear to be at this stage no longer in issue. That is, that children often didn't go to school, often had to stay in basements for their own protection. And therefore, the questioning is irrelevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This witness has told us that schools were functioning, that his father was working. And now we find that while the schools were working, he didn't go because, in practice, the schools were closed. It's a question of credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My friend misrepresents the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're misrepresenting the evidence. The witness testified that the schools did their best. Sometimes they had even classes of not more than ten minutes. Could you please indicate what -- so to that extent, if you're testing the credibility on this issue, you can only test what was the testimony of the witness and not something else. Could you please explain what the relevance is of this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the relevance is the following: This witness says that he doesn't know where the school is when I asked him where his father was working. Even if it worked for a few minutes, we simply note that he didn't go. So I'm just stating that he didn't tell us the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. AG, was the school that you were visiting the same school as the school where your father was working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I should like to continue with questions linked more specifically to the statement that you made about being shot at. How can you be certain, Witness, that it was not an accidental shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The wording of the question is such that it requires the witness to enter into the mind of the shooter, which clearly cannot be done. The witness's evidence is first-hand evidence of being shot and, to the best of his recollection, the circumstances as he observed them. The question, therefore, is inadmissible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness take off his headphones, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage, we have several testimonies telling us that a bullet went through the body of this person, an adolescent, and it destroyed a shop window, and we are told of the sound this made when the bullet hit the glass. We also have indications that the glass was broken, but he has just told us that he didn't see the hole, any broken glass on the ground. We also know that there was a restaurant next to this window, and we saw bullet impacts on that restaurant. So the next question is, was it possible that this person was not targeted but that the bullet ricocheted? And so I think that the question is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the problem raised by Mr. Ierace is whether the witness can know it. Of course, it's a very relevant question. But it's not a matter of whether the question is relevant but whether the witness is in a position to answer that question. But let me just see whether I can solve your problem. Mr. AG -- yes. Mr. AG, you have been hit by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know from where it was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether you were specifically targeted by the person who fired the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not be able to answer that question. You would have to ask the person who was shooting. I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm sorry. You said that the witness said that he didn't see the hole, but I would like to know where the witness said that. Because as far as I remember, he said that he didn't see any broken glass on the ground. On page 48/7, that's what he said. He didn't mention the hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was listening to another channel, Your Honour, and I remember asking whether this witness saw a hole on the photograph, and that he said no. But I will verify that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could assist, I agree with my learned colleague that the witness did say that he didn't see the hole. And that is page 48 at line 22. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry about the interruption, Your Honour, but that was as I remembered it. Do I have your permission to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I also thank my learned friend for finding the right reference point more quickly than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Right, Witness. You answered the question -- questions which you were asked by the President. And I will now rephrase my question in relation to this restaurant. Do you know if this restaurant Arijana was also hit by -- was also hit, whether directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I believe that my sister told me later on that fire was opened on that restaurant, too. But at that time, I wasn't there. I was in the hospital so that I can't know. And it was a long time ago so that I don't really remember all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back to the shot which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I ask you. It's half past 12.00 now. You used, I think, more than twice the time compared to the examination-in-chief. Could you tell us how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very little, very little. I just wanted to show the 360 degrees. Or we can do it right now, or perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say it's fair if you get a few more minutes. And if you would need that, we can do it now right away and then perhaps have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very good. I do not know how long will the technology request, but I'd like to see the 360-degree photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes, it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like us to start from here. I don't know who is helping me. Are you helping me? [In English] So we are going to the right, please. A little bit to the right. Move to the right. Could we stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, once again, we see the same parking as a short while ago. Can we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Could you please zoom in. And a little bit more to the right. May we -- stop. Stop. May we zoom in again. A little bit again. More. That's it. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we once again see this area here, and you yourself called it its name. Will you please repeat its name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I think this is Hrasno, a hill called Hrasno. That is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you know if at the time, that is, July 1994, 9-4, do you know if that particular area was split between the two opposed sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Can we move again to the right a little bit. Would you stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you once again see three or four skyscrapers, high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you also said that this area was called Cengic Vila; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. This area, Witness, is in front of the restaurant, and we can see one of its flower pots here on this side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend has put a proposition to the witness which, allowing for the fact that it's a two-dimensional view and some photographic distortion, I don't think is correct, that is that those are opposite the coffee-shop, but the witness has answered the question. Perhaps it's a matter for the Trial Chamber in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did not quite understand the gist of this objection, which is not my custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But Witness, isn't this in Cengic Vila? Is that the area of Cengic Vila?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, is this next to the entrance into the restaurant called Arijana and next to the window shop [as interpreted] of the shoe shop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, at the time of the incident, even though you were only 13 or 14 years, who had the control over these high-rise buildings that we see here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, you cannot tell me yes or no. Or was it perhaps interpreted? My question was: Who controlled these buildings, to your knowledge? Do you know who had the control over them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: The control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you stated a moment ago when you were asked -- that is, excuse me. The Prosecution asked a question. You said that you did not hear any kind of sound or shot. Do you remember that you said that about -- some time ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. That misrepresents the evidence. The witness did give evidence of hearing a sound but didn't recollect whether he heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not the sound of a shot, as far as my recollection goes. The sound of breaking glass, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we have to look at the page 22/14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Did you hear the sound of any shooting before you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were shot, say within about ten minutes before you were shot?" The answer was, "No." That's the sound of shooting. You're now talking about, "Did you hear any shot or sound?" That's not the same. So would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was exactly my question in French, "Did you hear the sound of a shot, of something that was fired?" And what I said in French, I mentioned the "ten minutes" in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your new question was that the witness didn't hear any shot or sound, and I think the objection was that the witness testified that he did not hear the sound of a shot but that doesn't exclude that he heard other sound. So would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked by the Prosecution awhile ago whether within ten minutes of your accident you heard any sound of a shot, and your answer was no. Are you confirming this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, can you likewise confirm that within ten minutes preceding your accident, you were not in the street concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: We were walking, so that I don't know. Perhaps for about five minutes I was riding around on my bicycle. We were just walking by and then we stopped or, rather, my mother and sister stopped in front of the building, and I still rode for about four or five minutes on my bicycle, and then I also fetched to a stop in front of the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Right. But for about five minutes before this, you were elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And my very last question, Mr. President: Do you know, Witness, please, if a police investigation was started in relation to the accident of the shooting at the Arijana restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in the hospital so that I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there any reason to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Could that be conveniently done after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you think you need more than one or two minutes, we will do it after the break. We'll have a break until 1.00. Mr. AG, we will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. The questions I have to ask may be construed as going beyond re-examination for more --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. I'm sorry that I have to interrupt, but it seems that the witness is indicating that he cannot hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I can't hear all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have problems hearing the interpretation. Now it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for drawing my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for more abundant caution, I intend to seek leave to ask further questions as examination-in-chief, subject to the usual opportunity afforded to the Defence to further cross-examine on the specific issue if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, did you make a number of statements to the investigators from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was one of those statements made on the 11th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I do not remember the date. I wouldn't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown a document. I ask the document not be placed on the ELMO because it has identifying features.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise, on the document, your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the document can be shown to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document - I'm sorry I have to interrupt Mr. Ierace - but the document in question is a document which I'm showing you which has several pages. Some of these are pages in Serbian which have not been translated. Once again, we do not have a translation here, so I do not know whether Mr. Ierace can provide us with an immediate translation of the -- there are several numbers. 4276 or 0890, and the other document. And thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, those pages are not relevant to the questions I'm about to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we just have a look at them. May I take it, Mr. Ierace, that it's just page 2 of the document that you're particularly interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And the document may be returned to Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked this question by my learned colleague during cross-examination. Question: "Do you know if this restaurant Arijana was also hit, whether directly or indirectly?" And you replied that your sister told you something later on. Is that correct? Do you remember being asked that question and giving such an answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you remember whether at any stage you spoke to the man from the coffee shop who took you in his car to receive medical treatment about shots being fired either into the cafe or in relation to where he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Before I was wounded or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: After you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No. All I remember is that that man drove me to the hospital, that is, first to the emergency clinic and then to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see him after he drove you to the emergency clinic and later to the hospital or was that the last time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I didn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will now read to you a sentence from a statement that you signed on the 11th of November, 1995, being 16 months after this incident. "The man from the coffee shop who took me to the hospital told me the bullet went above his head." Does that remind you that the man from the coffee shop who took you to the hospital told you those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At the time that you signed your statement, did you also sign an acknowledgement -- I withdraw that. At the time that you signed your statement, was it read to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember, believe me. It was such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember placing your signature on a part of the statement which -- I'll withdraw that. Do you remember whether at the time that you signed your statement there was an interpreter present, that is, someone who was interpreting both the document and words that were spoken to you and by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you had placed that sentence in your statement, in other words, if you had told the investigator those things, would it have been the truth at that stage? In other words, your recollection in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I'm not really getting the -- the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. I have read to you a sentence from your statement of November 1995, and you have told us that you no longer remember what that sentence says. You no longer remember the events which that sentence describes. Nevertheless, since it is a sentence from your statement, does it reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must object, because we've understood where Mr. Ierace is driving at. The witness said that he does not remember doing -- having -- saying this, and the witness has just answered no, but he has three or four times been asked the same question. Three times, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Ierace was not putting the same question to the witness. So the objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At the time that you made your statement, did you do your best to describe the events as you remembered them then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Have you any reason to doubt that the contents of your statement in November 1995 were true and to the best of your recollection in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I have no reason not to tell the truth, and all that I said was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That completes the further questioning, Mr. President. I have no further questions by way of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the questions put to the witness by Mr. Ierace are related to an earlier statement. Is there any reason to cross-examine the witness on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not -- no. I'm afraid -- I'm afraid, Mr. President, I'm afraid so. I'm afraid so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then -- please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have just said that you had no reason not to tell the truth with regard to your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you said in 1995, it would appear, that you had spoken with the driver and today you said, and under oath, under oath before this Chamber that you do not remember having spoken with that driver, what is it that we are supposed to believe? What is the truth, the true explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: The best explanation is that it was eight years ago, and I do not recall all the details. That is all that I can tell you. After all, a lot of time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will ask you yet another series of question -- or questions in relation to this bullet. Do you know if your mother has ever made a statement in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know what it is that your mother said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if your mother -- do you know if your mother spoke to you after the incident about the circumstances under which it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't worded in the best way. Let me rephrase it. Did you speak with your mother about the circumstances under which it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Why, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And did your mother confirm to you that she had also heard the bullet hit the window of the shoe shop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember talking about that. I simply do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you talk about it with your sister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- that your sister also said that she, too, had heard the bullet hit that window of the shoe shop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You do not know whether your sister said that or not? Is that how we are to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My last question: Do you know if somebody recovered that bullet, found that bullet, that hit you or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Chamber noticed that you went beyond the questioning in re-examination. We accepted that. The Judges might have some questions to you as well, Mr. AG. So first, it's Judge Nieto-Navia who will put one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The Defence asked you whether your father was in the street in which you were wounded. Your answer was: "I am not sure." And then you said: "I cannot say whether he was in the street or in the house." My question is exactly the same. Was your father in the street in which you were wounded? But I would like to be clear: In that street, not in the street in general.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Your answer is no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to you, Mr. AG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand correctly, you and your sister left Sarajevo in 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember in which month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: In the month of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at that point in time, before your departure, did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No. Because at the beginning of the war, the schools stopped working. It was only later that some schools were formed in homes or in certain areas. I don't know exactly because I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I'm talking about April until you left, did you go to school or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never went to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war. The war started in 1992. When the first barricades were erected in Sarajevo, the schools stopped working. Until April, until I left Sarajevo, I didn't go to school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I understand now. Until the beginning of the conflict, you went to school; but as of April, you stopped going to school. Do you remember the circumstances under which you left the town? Was it because of the conflict? How did you leave the city? If I understand, it was only with your sister, and your mother stayed behind with your father.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes. Our parents wanted us to go because there was shooting in Sarajevo. We all thought that this would last a month or two. So as to avoid us experiencing the fighting, they wanted us to leave for a month or two, because that is what we all thought, that the war would only last that long. And once it calmed down, that we should come back. That was the only reason why we left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. But was it easy to leave the city without any problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes, in those days. But later on, it wasn't so easy to leave. At the time we left, it was quite -- it wasn't easy, but it wasn't as difficult as it was later on when the war really gained momentum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm referring now to the incident. You spoke of a young man who took you in his car. I understand that you were in shock, and it's not easy to remember, but in your opinion, was he passing by, or was his car parked in the area where the accident took place? Do you remember a little bit the circumstances surrounding this young man and his car; whether he was passing by, driving by, or whether his car was parked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Before I was wounded, when we arrived at the place of the accident, I didn't pay attention to the cars parked in front. But when I was wounded, after the wounding, we entered the passageway. The man came out of this restaurant, and he carried me to his car. And it was only then that I saw that his car was parked in front of the restaurant. However, before the incident, I didn't pay attention. It was only after I was wounded when he took me to his car that I saw that it was parked there. I didn't know whether it was his or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my last question: You returned in June, if I understand correctly, June 1994. And this was during a period of cease-fire when the situation was calmed -- calm in the city, and your parents decided that it was time for you and your sister to return. Or something else? What were the circumstances of your return to the city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AG
utterances.text: Yes. The so-called "blue routes" were opened, so it was possible to leave the city and to enter the city. So our parents decided that we should come back. Before that, it was not possible to leave the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. AG, this concludes your testimony before the Tribunal. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and giving your testimony because you'll understand that it's important for the Judges to hear the answers to the questions put by both parties and by the Judges themselves to the witnesses and get the information from those who were present at these times and at these places. So therefore, I'd like to thank you again, and I wish you a safe trip home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. I take it that facial distortion will not be affected by...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before that happens, might I remind you that the only medical documentation that I rely upon in relation to this witness is, as I understand it, already an exhibit, that is, P2794. So there is no need to go through the medical documentation. Thank you. I should add, Mr. President, that in relation to the statement, I don't seek to tender that, provided the Defence concedes that the sentence I read is from a statement of the witness dated the 11th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard no objection, and usually when there's little reading of a part of a previous statement, this is accepted. Well, since the Defence itself referred to that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just checking the text I have in front of me. And you know that very often the Defence and the Prosecution agree, and this is one such case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3677 under seal, pseudonym sheet. Exhibit P3279WW, photograph marked by witness. Exhibit P3279W, 360-degree Quicktime movie. And Exhibit P3280WW, under seal, videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the 360-degree photograph, we still have the same objection and there is no reason for me to repeat it each time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The standing object against the 360-degree photograph. And all documents are admitted in evidence, including the tapes. Before you call your next witness -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, regarding exhibits, the medical documents, I have to say that one of those documents that we received relating to this witness is -- appears to be one of those that were in extremis. And again we go from white to grey-white. And by showing you this text, I want to show that it is not legible, at least, this part. It is only because the Defence once again wishes to stress that it was handicapped in the preparation of its cross-examination as a result of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have taken notice of that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Before we continue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'd like to address you on one issue. You reminded this witness, while questioning, two times that he gave his statement under oath. I'd invite you, if there's any need to remind a witness that he's under oath, that you ask for my intervention. Not because I find that it would under no circumstances be acceptable that a short reminder to the oath taken by the witness should be improper, but you used it while putting a question to the witness which we should believe, his statement given in 1995, that he speak -- that he spoke to the driver or that he testified under oath in this court that he did not remember having done so. Your suggestion was that we should believe either his statement at that time or his statement at this time. It's perfectly possible that what he remembered in 1995, he might not have remembered any more in 2002. Therefore, I think it was not proper to stress that he was under oath, because the suggestion that he might have lied under oath was of -- at least, that he -- we should choose to believe either one or the other is not correct. So therefore, I invite you to ask for my intervention whenever necessary under Rule 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for telling me that. Under no circumstances did I wish even to suggest that this witness was lying under oath, because if that had been my opinion, you would have known it very directly, and so would have he. I simply -- est enim usulandum affirmatum religiosa. What I mean is simply the following, Mr. President: This statement is made under oath and not the written statement. Therefore, I thought that, in law, there are two different weights to be given to these statements, and that is the only reason why I mentioned this. But I shall pay attention, and in the future, as always, I will ask for your assistance, your kind assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You suggested that a choice had to be made between what he said then and what he said today, and that suggestion was not right. Mr. Ierace, would you please call your next witness. Or would you say -- I don't know how much time you need to -- we lost already some of the time we gained. If you say we could easily deal with the witness tomorrow, we perhaps better could stop now, but if there's even the slightest doubt, tomorrow is the last day before the Easter weekend, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Stamp will be taking that witness, and we are of the opinion that this witness will be comfortably finished tomorrow. Whilst I'm on my feet, I indicate that I won't be present tomorrow, and I simply indicate that in case there is anything planned for tomorrow that might require my presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we have anything special in mind for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.35 p.m.,
